Colombia Total Peace Policy at a Crossroads

The ambitious total peace strategy faces mounting challenges from multiple directions.

The multi-track negotiation approach, unprecedented in its scope and ambition, has opened simultaneous dialogue with the ELN, FARC dissident factions, and several criminal organizations, stretching institutional capacity thin.

While the ELN talks in Havana have shown signs of progress on humanitarian matters, the core political issues of territorial governance and resource extraction remain deeply contentious and unresolved after multiple rounds of negotiation.

In departments like Arauca, Norte de Santander, and Cauca, communities report that ceasefire agreements have not translated into reduced violence on the ground, eroding public confidence in the peace process.

The international community role as facilitators and guarantors remains crucial but is complicated by geopolitical tensions that make coordination between guarantor countries (Cuba, Venezuela, Norway) increasingly difficult.

For the total peace policy to succeed, the government must prioritize achievable agreements with groups that show genuine willingness to transform, rather than pursuing parallel negotiations that dilute its negotiating leverage and institutional focus.
